newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.S. will pay dearly if it attacks Iraq - paper.
newsitem.headline: U.S. will pay dearly if it attacks Iraq - paper.

text.p: The United States will pay dearly if it attacks Iraq in reprisal for its sending of military helicopters into Western-declared no-fly zones, the official al-Iraq newspaper said on Wednesday.
"Here is the United States again giving a free rein to its aggressive policies and despotic practices against Iraq," the paper said in a front-page editorial.
"The United States will pay a heavy price if it carries out a new aggression or a new stupidity against Iraq."

The editorial was a reaction to remarks by U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen in which he said Washington would "respond appropriately" if Iraq went ahead and sent its helicopters into the southern no-fly zone.
Iraqi helicopters arrived on Tuesday at the southern border with Saudi Arabia to pick up Moslem pilgrims returning from Mecca.
Reporters taken in two helicopters to the border at Arar said they saw seven more helicopters parked three km (1.8 miles) from the border, waiting for the pilgrims to arrive.
It was the second time this month that Iraq had defied U.N. and Western restrictions on flights by its aircraft.
On April 9 it flew a civilian plane carrying 104 pilgrims to Saudi Arabia, defying a U.N. ban on international flights imposed after Iraqi troops invaded Kuwait in 1990.

The paper reiterated Iraq's long-standing position about the no-fly zones in southern and northern Iraq, saying they were illegally imposed by the United States and its allies following the 1991 Gulf War over Kuwait.

After the April 9 flight the U.N. Security Council issued a statement calling on Iraq not to fly more planes without its consent, but stopped short of calling it a breach of the embargo as sought by Washington.
"The U.S. failed drastically and was dealt a moral blow," al-Iraq said, commenting on the Security Council decision.
"It seems it (Washington) does not want to swallow its defeat and the deterioration of its standing and the shaking of its image at the United Nations and the Security Council.

"The masters of the White House have to understand that the time of issuing unfair and ready-made resolutions dictated by Washington against Iraq is gone forever and that a new era...is in the offing."
The government newspaper al-Jumhouriya published a similar commentary, saying statements by Cohen and President Bill Clinton on the issue of helicopters were a sign of weakeness and bankruptcy.
But it said this might not stop America from launching an aggression against Iraq though its options were feeble and limited this time.
Washington said on Tuesday he would not stop Iraq's helicopter movement of Moslem pilgrims through the southern no-fly zone, but warned Baghdad against building up its military forces in the area.
